story-001.text: This happened at the very beginning of my practice, when I, a doctor as yet unknown to anyone, spent my consulting hours in dreary solitude, pacing about my consulting room and moving one and the same object from place to place twenty times over. In the course of a whole month I had had only two patients: the yard-keeper of the house where I lived, and some passing stranger who suffered from nervous tics.

story-002.text: On the evening I am speaking of, an event took place: a new patient appeared, the third in all. Even now, when I close my eyes, I can see him before me as if he were alive. He was a man of middle height, bald, with an important, slightly absent gaze, a curly fair little beard and a sharp nose. His build betrayed a tendency to stoutness, which made something of a contrast with his abrupt, impulsive movements. I also noticed two peculiarities that would not be worth mentioning had they not pointed to a severe degree of nervous disorder: a convulsive twitching of the eyelids and a ceaseless working of the fingers. Whether he sat or walked, spoke or was silent, the fingers of his hands bent and unbent uncontrollably, as though tangled in an invisible, sticky cobweb.

story-003.text: I pretended to be entirely indifferent to his visit, keeping on my face that cold, attentive composure which, as it seemed to me then, belongs to any profession of the least seriousness. He grew embarrassed and sat down, blushing like a girl.

story-006.text: With an effort he glanced at me and frowned, studying the things on my writing desk. A minute later I heard his limp, embarrassed voice again:

story-007.text: “It’s a thing, you see, sir, of such a kind… A very strange… strange. A strange thing… One might say — a thing… But then, you won’t believe me.”

story-008.text: Intrigued, I looked at him closely; he was breathing slowly, with difficulty, his eyes lowered, evidently trying to concentrate on his own sensations.

story-009.text: “And why should I not believe you?”

story-010.text: “Just so, sir. It’s hard to believe,” he objected with conviction, suddenly raising to me his short-sighted, bewilderedly smiling eyes.

story-011.text: I shrugged. He was abashed and coughed softly, evidently preparing to begin his story. Several times his left hand rose to his face, plucking at his beard; the whole of him, so to speak, was bustling inwardly, turning something over. It showed especially in the strained play of his face, which burned now with despair, now with embarrassment. I did not hurry him, knowing from experience that in such cases it is better to wait than to urge.

story-012.text: At last the man began to speak and, having begun, grew almost calm. His voice sounded even and quiet, his face stopped twitching, and only the fingers of his left hand went on moving quickly and nervously, freeing themselves from the invisible cobweb.

story-013.text: “If I’m to astonish you, then astonish you I shall,” he said, as if with regret. “Only you… I beg you, sir… don’t interrupt me… Ye-es…”

story-014.text: “Don’t upset yourself,” I remarked gently. “Astonishment, after all, is the lot of the uninitiated.”

story-015.text: Having thus hinted at my supposed experience in the field of psychiatry, I assumed a relaxed pose — that is, I crossed my legs and began tapping a pencil against my fingertips. He faltered, sighed, and went on:

story-016.text: “Please, would you be so kind… if possible… every time I raise my hand… Forgive me… Would you trouble yourself to say, please: ‘Leipzig… International Tournament, sir… Mate in three moves’? Eh? Please.”

story-017.text: Before I had even managed to turn myself into an enormous question mark, his words came pouring out again — passionate, persuasive, quiet:

story-018.text: “I can’t, sir… Would you believe it? I don’t sleep, I don’t eat, I’m turning into an idiot… I need it to take my mind off things, that’s what, sir! The moment you say those words, I’ll calm down… You talk and you talk, and then up it floats, that very thought… I’m afraid of it. Now, if you’d be so good as to listen… It must have been, oh, eight or nine days ago… Of course, we all think about it… This one will die, then another… About death, I mean… And how it all comes about, I tell you, how one thing hooks onto the next — it’s beyond all understanding… There I was, sitting by the window, reading a book, only I hadn’t much wish to read; it was getting on towards dinner. I sit there and I look… You know the kind of mood one gets into — at another moment I’d have spat and paid no attention… But just then my thoughts were wandering, it was warmish, such a quiet summer day… And along comes, I see, a woman with a babe in arms, a kerchief on her of red calico, bright red… Then a little girl of about seven ran past, a skinny little thing, with a ginger pigtail sticking out like a piglet’s tail… Allow me, sir… Then I see a gymnasium schoolgirl going by after her, then a lady, a very well-dressed lady, very proper, and behind her, if you please — a little old woman… There… you understand?”

story-019.text: I looked at his hands with curiosity: they were trembling, quickly and finely, unbuttoning and buttoning a button of his frock coat. In what he was telling me there evidently lay, for him, a whole chain of frightening conclusions.

story-020.text: “No, I don’t understand,” I said, “but go on.”

story-021.text: He was very pale and was looking somewhere off to the side, beyond the portière. I smiled encouragingly; he winced, thought a moment, and went on:

story-022.text: “When the old woman had gone by, this notion comes into my head: why, now all that’s missing is a funeral procession… I stepped away from the window, but I keep thinking: you too, brother, will die… well, and everything of that sort. And then I think: but who are we all, living, walking and talking? Not just ripening corpses, like apples on a bough — there is something more in all of it, a kind of terrible simplicity…”

story-023.text: Before the last two words his voice broke with agitation. I listened intently.

story-024.text: “None of this,” he continued, “spoiled my appetite. After dinner I even lay in the hammock, with pleasure… But when night came on — enough to make you cry for help — I’m going out of my mind, and that’s all there is to it!”

story-025.text: A pitiful smile froze on his convulsively intent, sweating face. Pulling out a handkerchief and blowing his nose, he went on looking me in the face with the same fixed, petrified stare.

story-026.text: I smiled in spite of myself: that small detail, the handkerchief, suddenly broke the slightly eerie impression made on me by this strange man who had taken fright at something. But he went on with his story, and soon I again felt myself in the grip of a sharp, morbid curiosity. Not yet knowing what the matter was, I was, it seems, already prepared to believe this man, leaving his abnormality in doubt.

story-027.text: He put away the handkerchief and went on:

story-028.text: “Until evening I was calm… I even went about cheerful… Well, before going to bed I stepped out into the little garden as usual, to have a look about, to smoke a cigarette. Quiet; the stars burning somehow peculiarly — not softly and kindly, but irritating me, troubling me…

story-029.text: “I sit, I think… About what? About eternity, death, the mystery of the universe, space… well, about everything that creeps into your head after a hearty supper and strong tea… I remember the philosophers, various theories, conversations… And one thing came back to me, from my childhood days… I was very proud of it then, that I had arrived at it, so to speak, by my own wits. This is how I reasoned: an infinite amount of time went by before ‘I’ appeared… Well, sir, I die, and let us suppose I never existed at all… And so — why, within the bounds of infinity, can I not appear again? I put it a little confusedly, of course… but an example… like this… a clean sheet of paper, say, here. I take a pencil and write 10. And now — I go and rub it out completely, clean away… And what then! I take the pencil again and write ‘10’ again. You understand — a 1 and a 0.”

story-030.text: He fell silent, caught his breath, and wiped with his sleeve the drops of sweat that glistened peacefully on his tormented bald skull.

story-031.text: “Go on,” I said, “and don’t stop. In such cases it is better to tell everything at once; it’s easier.”

story-032.text: “Yes,” he caught up, “I… and… well, that’s not the point… So then. My thoughts kept spinning without stopping, as if some whirlwind had caught them up… And it was here, for the first time, that the terrible thought came to me that one could know everything, if…”

story-033.text: “If?” I prompted, seeing that he had suddenly stopped.

story-034.text: He answered in a whisper, solemn and despondent:

story-035.text: “If one thinks about it without stopping, without fear of death.”

story-036.text: I shrugged, keeping on my face a polite readiness to listen further. My patient squirmed convulsively in his chair, evidently stung.

story-037.text: “Unbelievable?” he exclaimed. “But what if I show you such a prospect: you, yes, you, Doctor, all at once, suddenly, sitting in that armchair, remember that there is infinite space?.. Very well, sir… But you think of it with walls, don’t you — you put walls around that space in your mind! And suddenly there is nothing for you, no walls, and you feel with all the cold of your heart what sort of thing it is — space! Only a single instant, yes, sir, but that very instant can lay you out dead, because you are — not fitted for it!..”

story-038.text: “Possibly,” I said. “But I cannot even imagine…”

story-039.text: “Exactly!..” he caught up with morbid triumph. “Nor could I imagine it, but I feel it”—and he struck his chest with his fist—“here, I carry such a feeling that the moment I think about it intently, without tearing myself away, I shall understand… And having understood — I shall die. That’s why a while ago I asked you to shout the words ‘mate in three moves’ if I raise my hand… It’s all because with those very words, at the critical moment, when it is already beginning to close in, you will at once give my thoughts another direction.

story-040.text: “And that problem in three moves I fished out back when I used to take a certain little magazine. The moment I hear your voice, I’ll set about solving it — straight off, at full gallop… Well then, sir… I’m sitting there, and suddenly I hear my wife calling me from the porch: ‘Misha!’ And I hear that she’s calling, but answer her, imagine, I cannot — my tongue was fettered, and that was that… Only later did I guess what the trick of it was: my mood at that moment was, so to speak, the most unearthly, a rare mood even, and here I’d have to talk about some household matter, all sorts of trifles. I keep silent. She calls a second time: ‘Mi-isha! Have you fallen asleep, or what?’ Then I lost my temper and said to her — forgive me — these very rude words: ‘Go to the devil!’ Very well, sir. She went away. And I grew so sad after that, I can’t even tell you. I’ll go to bed, I think. I undressed, lay down, but still I can’t sleep; all sorts of circles flicker, glowing flies go running… And my heart, I must tell you, has long been out of order… And so it began to play all sorts of tricks… Now it stops, now it strikes like a drumroll, so hard that there isn’t air enough… Fear took hold of me, I broke into a fever… I’m dying, I think to myself… And as soon as I thought it, the bed floated away beneath me, and I can’t feel myself at all… Well, all right. It passed, I came to… but I can’t sleep any longer… All sorts of thoughts run on, run like dogs in the street, all sorts of images flicker, memories… Then I see the little girl from the morning walking, after her the young lady, then the old woman… that whole procession moves along as if alive… And no sooner, you know, had my thought stopped on that old woman than I began to tremble and shouted at the top of my voice: I feel that one more turn of thought, and I shall understand — you understand — I shall understand and solve the whole riddle of death and life, as plainly as two times two is four… And I feel that the moment I understand it, in that very same moment… I shall die… I shall not bear it.”

story-041.text: He fell silent, and it seemed to me that the room itself sighed, catching its breath noisily and convulsively. White as lime, the frightened man sat before me, not taking his glassy, bulging eyes from my face. And suddenly, with a careful, clumsy movement, he raised his hand, stretching it upward — the sign of approaching horror — a hand with a starched cuff and a bronzed cufflink.

story-042.text: And at that moment, I suppose, there were two madmen in the room — he and I. His panic infected me; I lost my head, forgetting both ‘mate in three moves’ and what that helpless hand, flung upward with its yellow fingers, meant. Without a thought, with a single unbearably blazing desire to jump up and run, I stared into his eyes as they slowly sank back into the depths of their sockets — small black abysses, going out irresistibly and aimlessly…

story-043.text: The hand was coming down. Lazily it bent, first at the wrist, then at the elbow, then at the shoulder; it swayed, and quietly fell, its palm softly slapping against the bend of his knee.

story-044.text: Fright brought my memory back. I leapt up and cried out in a measured, firm voice, trying not to seem ridiculous to myself:

story-045.text: “Leipzig! International Tournament! Mate in three moves!”

story-046.text: He did not stir. Dead, his face at peace, flooded with electric light, he went on gazing, motionless and stern, at that point above the back of my armchair where, a minute before, my eyes had been shining.
